readerTitle: Rewrite a landing page that nobody acts on
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소상공인 대상 기장 대행 회사, 대기업 인사팀의 사내 멘토링 페이지) + 실제 연구 1건 (Cialdini의 국립공원 표지판 연구). 모든 수치는 설명용입니다.
insight: 랜딩 페이지를 고칠 때는 문구를 더 멋지게 다듬기보다 두 가지를 먼저 본다. 방문자가 무엇과 비교하게 되는지(프레이밍), 그리고 자기와 비슷한 누가 이미 하고 있는지(사회적 증거)다.
misconception: 랜딩 페이지가 안 먹히는 이유는 회사 소개가 부족해서다. 이용자 수처럼 큰 숫자를 보여주기만 하면 사회적 증거가 된다.

sources.text: Cialdini, R. B. (2003). Crafting Normative Messages to Protect the Environment. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 12(4).
기장 대행 회사, 사내 멘토링 프로그램, 가격과 인원 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Petrified Forest 국립공원 연구: '많은 방문객이 나무 화석을 가져간다'는 표지판이 오히려 절도를 늘렸다는 결과입니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다. 게시 전에 원문(Cialdini 2003; Cialdini et al. 2006, Social Influence)으로 다시 확인하세요.
MKT-03-09(호텔 수건 연구)와 겹치지 않도록 수건 연구는 다루지 않았습니다. 이 레슨은 새 개념 없이 MKT-03-01(사회적 증거)과 MKT-03-06(프레이밍)만 적용합니다.

cards.title: A page that talks only about itself
body: A small bookkeeping firm serves local business owners. Its landing page says: "Full-service accounting solutions since 2009. Contact us for pricing. Trusted by hundreds."

Hundreds of owners visit each month. Almost none book a call. Nothing on the page is false. It just never answers the visitor's quiet questions: *compared to what?* and *is anyone like me doing this?*

image.label: A plain landing page with a visitor shrugging
image.brief: 노트북 화면 속 단조로운 랜딩 페이지. 'Full-service accounting solutions', 'Contact us for pricing' 같은 문구. 화면 앞의 가게 주인이 영수증 더미를 들고 어깨를 으쓱함. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should the page show the price?
body: The service costs $400 a month. Most visitors do their own books today, usually on weekends.
You decide to show the price instead of hiding it. Which version do you put on the page?

options.feedback: **Framing** at work, against you. A big yearly lump becomes the number visitors compare everything to, before they see what they get.

options.text: "$400 a month. Less than what a lost weekend of receipts costs you."
options.feedback: **Framing** done well. You set the comparison to something the owner already pays: their own time. Same price, a reference point that fits their problem.
This shrinks the number, which is a kind of **framing**. But it compares the service to a sandwich, not to the owner's real problem, and sounds like a consumer ad.

cards.title: Which proof goes under the headline?
body: Most visitors run cafés, trades and small clinics. They are unsure whether handing over their books is worth it. Pick one block of proof.

options.feedback: It is **social proof**, but vague. The visitor can't tell whether those hundreds look anything like their own business.

options.text: Three short quotes from a café owner, a plumber and a dental practice, with first names and business type
options.feedback: **Social proof** works best when the others look like you. Each visitor can find someone in their own shoes.

options.text: "Most small businesses fall behind on their books. You're not alone."
options.feedback: This is **social proof** for the wrong behavior. It comforts visitors by telling them falling behind is normal, which removes the reason to act.

cards.title: Same firm, same price, a new page.

breakdown.label: "Full-service solutions since 2009"
breakdown.detail: Now: "Get your weekends back. We'll do the books."

breakdown.label: "Contact us for pricing"
breakdown.detail: Now: "$400 a month, less than a lost weekend"

breakdown.label: "Trusted by hundreds"
breakdown.detail: Now: three owners who run businesses like the visitor's

cards.callout: Nothing about the service changed. Only what visitors compare it to, and who they see using it.
cards.softwareNote: On a software pricing page, the same edits apply. "$29 per seat" can be framed against the hours of manual work it replaces, and proof works best from companies of the visitor's size and industry.

cards.title: Two ideas from this unit did the work.
body: **Framing:** people judge a number by what sits next to it. The firm didn't lower the price. It chose the comparison.
**Social proof:** when people are unsure, they look at what others like them do. Who those others are matters more than how many.

Proof can backfire, too. In a study at Petrified Forest National Park, a sign saying many visitors took petrified wood was linked to *more* theft, not less. Telling people a bad habit is common makes it feel acceptable.

image.label: A price tag next to a weekend calendar, and three similar faces
image.brief: 화면을 둘로 나눈 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: '$400' 가격표 옆에 영수증에 묻힌 주말 달력(비교 기준). 오른쪽: 카페 주인, 배관공, 치과 직원 세 사람의 말풍선. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A better page can still break trust.
body: The frame has to be true for most customers. If the service still eats owners' weekends, "get your weekends back" is a promise you will break in month one.
Proof has to be real, recent and used with permission. Made-up or stale quotes are easy to spot and hard to recover from.
And change one thing at a time if you can. If four edits go live at once, you won't know which one moved sign-ups.

cards.title: Now it's an internal page.
body: You're on the People team at a company of 900. Six weeks ago you launched a mentoring program: one hour a month with a senior colleague. So far, 30 people from Sales, Support and Finance have signed up.
You're rewriting the intranet page. What leads the page?

options.text: "Only 30 of 900 people have joined. Don't miss out!"
options.feedback: This is **social proof** pointing the wrong way. It tells 870 people that not joining is what almost everyone does.

options.text: "30 colleagues in Sales, Support and Finance are already in. Here's what two of them got from it."
options.feedback: The same true number, framed as *who* rather than *how few*. Readers see **social proof** from teammates they recognize.
Right idea to address time, but this **framing** picks a bigger-sounding total. "One hour a month" is the same commitment and feels lighter.

cards.softwareNote: An onboarding screen for a team tool has the same choice. "3 of your teammates already use this" beats "Only 5% of your company has set this up."

cards.title: Choose the comparison, then show people like them.
body: This lesson used two ideas from the unit: **framing**, to set what the price or effort is compared to, and **social proof**, to show similar people already acting. Neither changed the offer.
**Try it today:** open your own landing or sign-up page. Find one number with no comparison next to it and one proof line that doesn't say who. Rewrite both.
